Bunny Berigan first recorded the song in 1936 with a small group that included pianist Joe Bushkin, drummer Cozy Cole, and clarinetist Artie Shaw. That early version helped introduce the number to jazz audiences and gave Berigan a vehicle for the lyrical, dramatic trumpet style that would become closely associated with him.

The song itself had debuted the same year on Broadway in *The Ziegfeld Follies of 1936*. In that production, it was presented not as the brooding jazz ballad it later became, but as a duet patter number performed by Bob Hope and Eve Arden. Its transformation from a theatrical novelty into a deeply expressive jazz standard was largely shaped by Berigan’s interpretation.

By 1937, Berigan had re-recorded “I Can’t Get Started” in a big-band setting, and this version became his signature performance. His expansive trumpet introduction and emotional phrasing turned the song into one of the defining records of his career. From then on, “I Can’t Get Started” was closely identified with Berigan, standing as perhaps the most famous example of his ability to combine technical brilliance with a vulnerable, vocal-like expressiveness.

The song also intersects with the career of singer Lee Wiley. Wiley and Berigan were lovers for a time, and in 1936 they appeared together on her CBS radio feature, *Saturday Night Swing Club*. Given Wiley’s cool, intimate vocal style and her gift for understated emotional nuance, “I Can’t Get Started” would seem to have been a natural choice for her repertoire.

Yet Wiley recorded the song only once, and then only informally. Her lone known performance of “I Can’t Get Started” comes from a 1945 Town Hall concert, rather than from a studio session. That rarity adds a certain poignancy to the song’s place in her story: although it suited her artistry and was tied to someone with whom she had both a personal and musical connection, she left behind just a single informal version.

Written by Vernon Duke, with lyrics by Ira Gershwin, it was introduced in the 1936 edition of the *Ziegfeld Follies*. Like many songs of its era, it mixed romance with topical wit: the singer boasts of extraordinary accomplishments—travel, fame, political importance, even involvement in world events—only to confess that none of these triumphs helps in the one matter that counts, winning the attention of the beloved. Its references to contemporary history, including unrest in Spain during the period of the Spanish Civil War, helped root the song in the atmosphere of the 1930s.

The song’s most famous early interpreter was trumpeter and singer Bunny Berigan. Berigan first recorded “I Can’t Get Started” in 1936, and then made the definitive version in 1937. That later recording, with its dramatic trumpet introduction and weary, intimate vocal, transformed the song into his personal statement. Although Berigan was a brilliant jazz musician with a larger repertory, “I Can’t Get Started” became inseparable from his name. Its mixture of bravado and failure seemed to fit both his musical personality and, in retrospect, the tragedy of his short life and troubled career.

Lee Wiley’s connection to the song adds another layer of meaning. She did not leave behind a major studio interpretation of the tune in the way Berigan did. Because of her connection to Berigan, even this lone performance carries emotional weight.

Its Broadway origins, its topical 1930s references, its association with Berigan’s trumpet and voice, and Lee Wiley’s personal connection to that history all contribute to its lasting resonance. The song endures not simply as a standard, but as a work in which personal longing, jazz interpretation, and historical memory meet.

counterfactuals.output:
“I Can’t Get Started” is one of those songs that began as Broadway sophistication and became, largely through jazz musicians, a kind of tragicomic anthem.

## 1. The song’s origin

“I Can’t Get Started” was written in 1936 by **Vernon Duke** with lyrics by **Ira Gershwin**. It was introduced in the *Ziegfeld Follies of 1936*, commonly associated with **Bob Hope** in its original theatrical setting.

On paper it is a comic “list song”: the singer claims to have achieved absurdly grand things—

> I’ve flown around the world in a plane  
> I’ve settled revolutions in Spain  
> The North Pole I have charted  
> But I can’t get started with you

The joke is that the narrator is worldly, famous, powerful, heroic—yet helpless in love. That mixture of urbane wit and emotional defeat made it perfect for jazz interpretation.

Musically, Vernon Duke’s melody has a floating, slightly yearning quality, and the harmony gives improvisers plenty to work with. It is not just a novelty song; it has a genuinely melancholy core.

## 2. Bunny Berigan and the definitive jazz version

The trumpeter **Bunny Berigan** is the figure most responsible for making “I Can’t Get Started” a jazz standard.

Berigan recorded it more than once, but the famous version is his **1937 Victor recording** with **Bunny Berigan and His Orchestra**. It became his signature performance.

Why it mattered:

- **The opening trumpet cadenza** is one of the iconic moments of swing-era trumpet playing. It is bold, dramatic, and almost operatic.
- Berigan’s tone is huge but vulnerable: brilliant on top, with a slightly bruised emotional quality underneath.
- He also sings the lyric, not as a polished crooner but as a musician embodying the song’s rueful humor.
- The performance turns a witty Broadway song into something more personal and tragic.

Berigan’s life later gave the record an added poignancy. He was a spectacularly gifted trumpeter, admired by other musicians, but he struggled with alcoholism and died young in 1942. Because of that, “I Can’t Get Started” can sound almost autobiographical in retrospect: a man who can do astonishing things musically, but cannot quite “get started” in life.

The 1937 recording is often treated as one of the great documents of the swing era.

## 3. Billie Holiday’s version

**Billie Holiday** recorded “I Can’t Get Started” in 1938, during one of her great early periods, when she was making small-group records with musicians associated with Count Basie and the New York swing scene.

Holiday’s approach is very different from Berigan’s.

Berigan dramatizes the song; Holiday internalizes it.

She does not treat the lyric merely as a clever list of impossible accomplishments. In her hands, the boasts feel almost beside the point. What matters is the emotional punch of the final line: “I can’t get started with you.” She pares away the show-business cleverness and makes the song about frustration, longing, and romantic defeat.

Holiday was also a master of rhythmic placement. She could sing slightly behind the beat, bend a phrase, or understate a word so that the lyric sounded newly conversational. With her, “I Can’t Get Started” becomes less a comic confession and more a quiet admission of helplessness.

## 4. Why the lyric about Spain is strange

The line is:

> I’ve settled revolutions in Spain

To modern ears, this is odd for several reasons.

First, the song appeared in **1936**, the same year the **Spanish Civil War** began. That war became one of the defining political and humanitarian crises of the 1930s. So a light lyric about “settling revolutions in Spain” can feel strangely glib, especially knowing that Spain was about to enter, or had just entered, a brutal conflict that no one “settled” quickly.

Second, the lyric is deliberately absurd. Ira Gershwin is piling up impossible claims: flying around the world, charting the North Pole, being consulted by Franklin D. Roosevelt, having tea with Greta Garbo, and so on. “Settled revolutions in Spain” belongs to that comic fantasy of omnipotence. The singer is saying, in effect: “I can handle world history, but not romance.”

Third, Spain had already been associated in the early 1930s with political upheaval: the fall of the monarchy, the establishment of the Second Republic, labor conflicts, regional struggles, and attempted uprisings. So even before the full horror of the Civil War, “revolutions in Spain” would have sounded topical.

The strangeness comes from the collision between **Ira Gershwin’s witty topical hyperbole** and the grim historical reality that soon surrounded Spain. What was meant as urbane comic exaggeration now carries an accidental historical chill.

## 5. Why the song lasted in jazz

“I Can’t Get Started” survived because it works on several levels:

- as a clever Ira Gershwin lyric,
- as a harmonically attractive Vernon Duke melody,
- as a vehicle for trumpet bravura through Bunny Berigan,
- as an intimate vocal confession through Billie Holiday,
- and as a standard whose irony deepened over time.

Berigan made it heroic and heartbreaking. Holiday made it private and human. The Spain line reminds us that even a stylish popular song can accidentally preserve the anxieties and historical shadows of its moment.

counterfactuals.output:
In **1936**, in the glitter and nervous laughter of *Ziegfeld Follies of 1936*, Vernon Duke and Ira Gershwin’s “**I Can’t Get Started**” first appeared as a comic sophisticate’s aria of failure. Its speaker is the modern overachiever as romantic beggar: he has flown the world, conquered public life, mastered celebrity and finance, even “**settled revolutions in Spain**”—yet cannot begin the only campaign that matters. The joke is pure Depression-era fantasy: worldly triumph piled so high that heartbreak becomes the one impossible luxury.

Then came **Bunny Berigan**.

In **1937**, Berigan recorded the version that made the song immortal in jazz. What had been a Broadway list-song became, through his trumpet, a confession. His horn enters as if already remembering the melody from some better life: broad, burnished, heroic, but fraying at the edges. Berigan sings too, almost conversationally, but the trumpet is the true narrator. It turns Gershwin’s witty exaggerations into autobiography—an artist who can soar, dazzle, command a room, and still seem unable to save himself. The record became his signature, and later his epitaph: a brilliant ascent shadowed by personal decline, the title itself taking on a terrible double meaning.

By **1938**, **Billie Holiday** had drawn the song into her own climate. Where Berigan made it a grand romantic wound, Holiday made it intimate, skeptical, lived-in. She did not need to dramatize the lyric’s impossibilities; she simply let each phrase arrive slightly behind the beat, as though desire itself had become tired of explaining. In her hands, the song’s worldly boasts feel less like comedy than armor. The refrain—“I can’t get started with you”—is not a punch line but a verdict softly delivered.

In **1940**, **Lee Wiley** gave the song another life: urbane, smoky, poised. Wiley’s “I Can’t Get Started” belongs to the night room rather than the stage or the ballroom. Her phrasing has the cool intelligence of someone who understands the absurdity of romantic obsession and submits to it anyway. She restores some of the song’s original sophistication, but with jazz’s after-hours knowledge: wit now bruised, elegance now lonely.

And all the while, history kept rewriting the lyric.

The line about having “**settled revolutions in Spain**” began as a dazzling topical boast, written just before and during the era when Spain was becoming one of the central wounds of the century. After the Spanish Civil War and under **Franco’s dictatorship**, the phrase acquired a dangerous charge. In Franco-era Spain, references to revolution and to Spain’s recent political trauma were not neutral stage decoration; they could attract censorship or require alteration. Thus a throwaway Ira Gershwin joke became politically radioactive. The singer’s impossible résumé—once comic hyperbole—now brushed against forbidden memory.

So the chronology of “I Can’t Get Started” is also a history of changing weather:

**1936**: Broadway wit, cosmopolitan fantasy, romance as comic defeat.  
**1937**: Berigan’s trumpet turns the song into jazz tragedy.  
**1938**: Holiday makes it private, wounded, modern.  
**1940**: Wiley makes it elegant, nocturnal, knowing.  
**Franco-era Spain**: one lyric, once merely clever, becomes a reminder that songs travel through regimes as well as through singers.

“I Can’t Get Started” began as a brilliant list of worldly accomplishments undone by love. Jazz stripped away the list and kept the undoing.
